disease.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
disease.scientific_name: Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) / Sideropaenic Anaemia / Hypochromic Microcytic Anaemia
disease.category: Haematological Disease / Nutritional Deficiency / Metabolic Disorder

overview.description: Iron Deficiency Anaemia (IDA) is the most common nutritional deficiency and the most prevalent cause of anaemia worldwide — affecting approximately 1.2 billion people globally. It occurs when the body's iron stores are depleted to the point where haemoglobin synthesis is impaired, resulting in reduced red blood cell production and characteristic microcytic (small), hypochromic (pale) anaemia. Iron is not only essential for haemoglobin synthesis but also for myoglobin (muscle oxygen storage), numerous oxidative enzymes (cytochromes, catalase, peroxidase), DNA synthesis, and immune function — explaining why IDA causes symptoms far beyond simple anaemia, including fatigue, cognitive impairment, reduced immunity, and characteristic iron-specific features such as pica (craving non-food items), koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), and glossitis. The causes span three fundamental mechanisms: inadequate dietary iron intake, pathological blood loss (the most common cause in adults), and impaired iron absorption.
overview.affected_organ: Blood (erythropoiesis — red blood cell production in bone marrow), but systemic effects on all organs due to reduced oxygen delivery and iron-dependent enzyme deficiency
overview.prevalence: WHO estimates 1.2 billion people affected globally; anaemia affects 1.62 billion people total (25% of world population); IDA accounts for approximately 50% of all anaemia cases. India: one of the highest burdens globally — 53% of women aged 15-49 and 58% of children under 5 years are anaemic (NFHS-5, 2021). Globally highest in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
overview.age_group: All ages affected; highest prevalence in: infants and young children (6-24 months); adolescent girls; pregnant and reproductive-age women; elderly. Can affect men of any age if blood loss or malabsorption is present.
overview.sex_ratio: Women affected 2-3x more than men in reproductive age due to menstrual blood loss and pregnancy demands; men and postmenopausal women with IDA must always be investigated for GI blood loss (potential malignancy).
overview.key_fact: In men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anaemia is ALWAYS a red flag that requires investigation for underlying GI blood loss — colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, or other pathology must be excluded urgently

iron_physiology.total_body_iron: Normal adult contains approximately 3-5g of iron: ~2/3 in haemoglobin (Hb); ~25% stored as ferritin and haemosiderin (liver, spleen, bone marrow); ~15% in myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes; ~0.1% as plasma iron bound to transferrin
iron_physiology.absorption_physiology: Iron is absorbed predominantly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Haem iron (from meat — Fe²⁺ within porphyrin ring) is absorbed directly via HCP1 transporter — 15-35% absorbed. Non-haem iron (Fe³⁺ from plant sources) must first be reduced to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome b reductase (Dcytb) — 2-20% absorbed (highly variable, enhanced by Vitamin C and inhibited by phytates, tannins, calcium). Fe²⁺ enters enterocytes via DMT-1 (divalent metal transporter-1). Exported from enterocytes to blood via ferroportin. Transported in blood bound to transferrin (apotransferrin when empty; transferrin when carrying iron). Delivered to bone marrow erythroblasts via transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) for haemoglobin synthesis.
iron_physiology.hepcidin_regulation: Hepcidin (produced by liver) is the master iron regulatory hormone. Hepcidin binds ferroportin → causes its internalisation and degradation → reduces iron export from enterocytes and macrophages into blood → reduces serum iron. Hepcidin RISES with: iron overload; inflammation (IL-6 stimulus) → explains why anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) has high hepcidin → iron trapped in stores. Hepcidin FALLS with: iron deficiency → allows maximum iron absorption. EPO (erythropoietin) suppresses hepcidin — allows iron mobilisation for increased erythropoiesis.

stages_of_IDA.description: Iron stores (ferritin) begin to fall; bone marrow iron stainable iron disappears; no change in serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, or Hb; no symptoms
stages_of_IDA.lab_findings: Ferritin low (<30 ng/mL); serum iron normal; TIBC normal; transferrin saturation normal; Hb NORMAL

stages_of_IDA.description: Iron stores depleted; serum iron falls; transferrin rises (TIBC rises); transferrin saturation falls; erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted; Hb may still be normal or just below normal
stages_of_IDA.lab_findings: Ferritin very low (<12 ng/mL); serum iron low; TIBC elevated (>400 µg/dL); transferrin saturation low (<16%); RDW elevated (anisocytosis); reticulocyte Hb content low; Hb normal or borderline low

stages_of_IDA.description: Hb falls below normal; RBCs become microcytic (small, MCV <80 fL) and hypochromic (pale, MCH <27 pg); classic symptoms of anaemia + iron-specific features develop
stages_of_IDA.lab_findings: Ferritin very low (<12 ng/mL); serum iron low (<60 µg/dL); TIBC high (>400 µg/dL); transferrin saturation <16%; Hb low; MCV low (<80 fL); MCH low (<27 pg); RDW elevated; peripheral blood film: microcytic hypochromic cells, pencil cells, target cells

types.name: IDA Secondary to Chronic Blood Loss
types.description: The most common cause of IDA in adults — the body cannot replace iron lost through chronic bleeding as fast as it is lost. In women of reproductive age: menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) is the leading cause. In men and postmenopausal women: gastrointestinal blood loss (peptic ulcer, colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, angiodysplasia, hookworm infestation) is the primary cause and ALWAYS requires urgent investigation.
blood_loss_sources: GI bleeding: peptic ulcer (H. pylori/NSAID), colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, colitis, coeliac disease, IBD, angiodysplasia
Hookworm and other GI parasites (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) — a major cause in tropical countries including India
types.clinical_importance: IDA in a man or postmenopausal woman IS a red flag requiring URGENT colonoscopy and upper GI endoscopy to exclude GI malignancy

types.name: IDA Secondary to Inadequate Dietary Iron Intake
types.description: Insufficient dietary iron to meet the body's demands. Common in: exclusively plant-based (vegetarian/vegan) diets (non-haem iron is less bioavailable); infants fed exclusively cow's milk beyond 6 months (low iron content); poverty and food insecurity; restrictive eating disorders; fad diets; elderly with poor appetite.
types.iron_bioavailability: Haem iron (meat, poultry, fish): 15-35% absorbed. Non-haem iron (plant foods): 2-20% absorbed depending on dietary context. Vegetarians and vegans absorb less iron from equivalent dietary iron intake — they are recommended to consume 1.8x the normal iron RDA.
high_risk_groups: Infants exclusively fed cow's milk >6 months (poor iron content)
Toddlers with excessive cow's milk intake (>500mL/day — displaces iron-rich foods)
Elderly with poor appetite and limited diet variety
Populations dependent on staple diets low in animal products (India — rice/wheat dominated diet)

types.name: IDA Secondary to Malabsorption
types.description: Iron absorption in the duodenum and proximal jejunum is impaired by several conditions — resulting in IDA despite adequate dietary intake. Must be actively sought when IDA does not respond to oral iron therapy.
causes: Coeliac disease — small intestinal villous atrophy destroys duodenal and proximal jejunal absorptive surface (the primary iron absorption site); IDA is the presenting feature in up to 50% of adult coeliac disease patients
Helicobacter pylori gastritis — H. pylori competes with host for iron; disrupts gastric acid production (acid is needed for Fe³⁺ reduction to Fe²⁺)
Atrophic gastritis — loss of gastric acid secretion (hypochlorhydria) impairs Fe³⁺ reduction and iron absorption
PPI (proton pump inhibitor) use — reduces gastric acid → reduces non-haem iron absorption by ~30-60%
Gastric bypass surgery (Roux-en-Y) — bypasses duodenum and proximal jejunum → dramatically reduces iron absorption; IDA affects 30-50% of gastric bypass patients long-term
Sleeve gastrectomy — less severe than RYGB but still impairs iron absorption
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease) — mucosal inflammation in duodenum/jejunum

types.name: IDA in Pregnancy
types.description: Iron requirements increase dramatically in pregnancy — from 18 mg/day to 27 mg/day — to support: (1) expansion of maternal red cell mass (~450mL blood volume expansion); (2) fetal iron needs (~270mg transferred to fetus); (3) placental iron needs (~90mg); (4) birth blood losses. Most pregnant women cannot meet this demand from diet alone and require supplementation. IDA in pregnancy is associated with: low birth weight, preterm birth, postpartum haemorrhage, maternal mortality, and impaired fetal brain development.
types.prevalence: IDA affects approximately 30-50% of pregnancies in India (NFHS data). Global prevalence: 38% of pregnant women anaemic (WHO).
types.trimester_variation: Physiological dilutional anaemia (pseudoanaemia) in 2nd trimester — haemodilution from plasma volume expansion; Hb nadir at 28-30 weeks; distinguishing IDA from physiological dilution requires ferritin levels

types.name: IDA in Infants and Children
types.description: Infants have very high iron demands for rapid brain development and growth. Neonates are born with iron stores from maternal transfer (third trimester — term infants have adequate stores for 4-6 months; premature infants have fewer stores). After 4-6 months, breast milk becomes insufficient in iron → dietary sources essential. Most common nutritional deficiency in children worldwide. Impairs cognitive development, learning, and physical growth.
highest_risk_periods: Full-term infants 4-12 months: iron stores depleted; breast milk insufficient; complementary foods not introduced or inadequate
Premature infants: lower iron stores at birth; higher demand for catch-up growth
Toddlers 1-3 years: excessive cow's milk intake (displaces iron-rich foods)
Adolescent girls: rapid growth + onset of menstruation
types.india_context: NFHS-5 (2019-21): 67% of children 6-59 months in India are anaemic — among the highest rates globally; exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months followed by iron-rich complementary foods is key national public health strategy

types.name: Functional Iron Deficiency / Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD) + IDA
types.description: In chronic inflammatory conditions (chronic kidney disease, heart failure, cancer, HIV, IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis), elevated hepcidin (stimulated by IL-6) sequesters iron in macrophages and reduces intestinal iron absorption — creating 'functional iron deficiency' (iron trapped in stores, unavailable for erythropoiesis) PLUS may coexist with true IDA from blood loss or reduced intake. Important distinction: ferritin is elevated in ACD (acute phase reactant) even when absolute iron stores may also be depleted — making ferritin unreliable; sTfR/ferritin ratio and bone marrow biopsy help distinguish.
types.differentiation_from_pure_IDA: Ferritin: low in IDA (<30); NORMAL or HIGH in ACD (false elevation due to acute phase); sTfR elevated in IDA, normal in ACD; bone marrow stainable iron absent in IDA, present in ACD; serum hepcidin: low in IDA, high in ACD

types.name: Refractory/Non-Responsive IDA
types.description: IDA failing to respond adequately to appropriate oral iron therapy (Hb rise <1g/dL/month or <2g/dL after 4 weeks). Causes: patient non-compliance (most common — GI side effects drive non-adherence); inadequate dose or duration; ongoing blood loss exceeding replacement; malabsorption (coeliac, H. pylori, bariatric surgery); iron refractory iron deficiency anaemia (IRIDA — rare genetic disorder: TMPRSS6 mutations causing constitutively elevated hepcidin); misdiagnosis (ACD, thalassaemia, other haemoglobinopathy).
types.management: Evaluate compliance; screen for H. pylori; coeliac serology; reassess ongoing blood loss; IV iron (bypasses GI absorption issues); IRIDA (genetic testing — IV iron required)

severity_levels.name: Mild Iron Deficiency (Ferritin Depleted — No Anaemia)
severity_levels.description: Iron stores depleted (low ferritin) but haemoglobin still within normal range; Stage 1-2 iron deficiency
severity_levels.symptoms: Minimal or absent; possibly subtle fatigue or reduced exercise tolerance; iron-specific symptoms (pica, restless legs) may be present
severity_levels.functional_impact: Often unrecognised; may have subtle cognitive impairment
severity_levels.management: Oral iron supplementation; dietary iron optimisation; identify and address underlying cause

severity_levels.name: Mild Iron Deficiency Anaemia
severity_levels.description: Haemoglobin mildly below normal; symptomatic but functional
severity_levels.MCV: Borderline low (75-80 fL) or normal early
severity_levels.symptoms: Fatigue; mild exertional dyspnoea; pallor; slight decrease in exercise tolerance; headache
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild — able to carry out daily activities with some effort
severity_levels.management: Oral ferrous sulphate or equivalent; dietary counselling; investigate cause; recheck FBC in 4-6 weeks

severity_levels.name: Moderate Iron Deficiency Anaemia
severity_levels.description: Haemoglobin significantly reduced; clear anaemia symptoms affecting daily function
severity_levels.MCV: Low (<78 fL); MCH low (<27 pg); MCHC low
severity_levels.symptoms: Significant fatigue and weakness; dyspnoea on mild exertion; palpitations; pallor of conjunctiva, nail beds, and palmar creases; possible koilonychia, glossitis, angular stomatitis
severity_levels.functional_impact: Moderate — daily activities significantly limited; work performance reduced
severity_levels.management: Oral iron (higher dose); investigate and treat cause urgently; consider IV iron if non-compliant or malabsorption; GP review

severity_levels.name: Severe Iron Deficiency Anaemia
severity_levels.description: Haemoglobin very low; significant physiological compromise; risk of cardiac complications
severity_levels.MCV: Markedly low (<70 fL); RBCs small and very pale; pencil cells, target cells on film
severity_levels.symptoms: Severe fatigue even at rest; dyspnoea at rest or on minimal exertion; palpitations and tachycardia at rest; angina (demand ischaemia from high-output state); possible cardiac flow murmur; significant pallor; possible oedema from high-output heart failure; headache; cognitive impairment
severity_levels.management: IV iron (most cases); blood transfusion if haemodynamically compromised, pre-operatively, or symptomatic cardiac compromise; hospital assessment; urgent investigation of cause

severity_levels.name: Very Severe / Life-Threatening Iron Deficiency Anaemia
severity_levels.description: Critically low haemoglobin; haemodynamic compromise; immediate risk to life
severity_levels.symptoms: Symptoms at rest; high-output heart failure; severe tachycardia; chest pain; confusion; syncope; possible multi-organ dysfunction from tissue hypoxia
severity_levels.management: Emergency hospital admission; blood transfusion (2-4 units packed red cells); cardiac monitoring; treat underlying cause urgently; IV iron post-transfusion to replenish stores

causes.pathophysiology_overview: IDA develops when iron losses + demands exceed iron absorption. Chronic negative iron balance first depletes stored iron (ferritin), then reduces serum iron and transferrin saturation, and finally impairs erythropoiesis causing falling Hb with characteristic microcytic hypochromic morphology.

primary_causes.category: Blood Loss (Most Common Cause in Adults)

subcauses.detail: The leading cause of IDA in premenopausal women globally. Normal menstrual loss: 30-40mL blood per cycle (15-20mg iron). Menorrhagia: >80mL per cycle → iron loss of 40+mg per cycle → chronic negative iron balance. Causes of menorrhagia: uterine fibroids, adenomyosis, endometriosis, hormonal dysfunction, IUDs, coagulation disorders. Treat both IDA AND menorrhagia.
subcauses.mechanism: Each mL of blood contains ~0.5mg iron; 80mL menstrual loss = 40mg iron lost per month

subcauses.detail: The most common cause of IDA in MEN and POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN — always warrants urgent investigation to exclude malignancy. Sources: peptic ulcer (H. pylori, NSAIDs); colorectal cancer (can cause occult blood loss with no overt bleeding); gastric cancer; inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); angiodysplasia (arteriovenous malformations — especially in elderly); intestinal polyps; diverticular disease; oesophageal varices; coeliac disease; GI parasites (hookworm).
subcauses.india_context: Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) infestation remains a significant cause of chronic GI blood loss and IDA in rural India and tropical areas — each hookworm consumes 0.03-0.15mL blood/day; heavy infestation causes significant daily blood loss
subcauses.red_flag: ANY man or postmenopausal woman with IDA requires upper GI endoscopy + colonoscopy to exclude malignancy

subcauses.detail: Each whole blood donation loses approximately 200-250mg iron. Regular donors (especially women) can develop IDA — minimum iron stores required before donation
Rare cause — visible or microscopic haematuria from renal stone, bladder cancer, glomerulonephritis

Non-haem iron (plant-based) is 2-8x less bioavailable than haem iron (animal-based). Vegetarians require 1.8x the normal iron RDA. Phytates in grains and legumes further reduce absorption. However, with careful dietary planning (combining iron-rich plants with Vitamin C, using iron cookware, soaking legumes), adequate iron status can be maintained.
subcauses.india_context: India's largely vegetarian diet (for religious, economic, and cultural reasons) is a major contributor to the high national IDA burden

subcauses.detail: Poverty limiting access to meat, fish, and diverse iron-rich foods; dependency on iron-poor staple diets
Breast milk iron (0.3mg/L) insufficient beyond 4-6 months; cow's milk low in iron AND inhibits iron absorption; exclusively breastfed or cow's milk-fed infants from 4-12 months at high risk

Most important cause of IDA from malabsorption in adults; duodenal villous atrophy destroys the primary iron absorption surface; IDA may be the ONLY presenting feature; gluten-free diet slowly restores absorption but IV iron often needed initially

H. pylori competes directly with host for iron (uses iron for its own growth); stimulates inflammatory cytokines reducing hepcidin; disrupts gastric acid (required for iron solubilisation); H. pylori eradication improves IDA even without other interventions in some patients
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass bypasses duodenum and proximal jejunum → greatest iron malabsorption; sleeve gastrectomy: moderate; requires IV iron and high-dose oral supplementation lifelong
Gastric acid required for Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ reduction (enabling DMT-1 absorption); PPIs reduce iron absorption 30-60%; avoid PPIs at time of oral iron dosing (separate by at least 2-4 hours)
Requirements increase from 18mg to 27mg/day; total extra iron needed 800-1000mg across pregnancy
Iron secreted in breast milk — but reduced by cessation of menstruation (net iron balance often neutral or positive)
Growth spurts dramatically increase iron demand — especially prematurity and adolescent girls with menstruation onset
EPO and ESAs for CKD, cancer — drive rapid RBC production depleting iron stores quickly; concurrent IV iron essential

risk_factors: Infancy (especially premature infants and formula-fed) and early childhood
Vegetarian or vegan diet without careful iron planning
Tropical/endemic areas with hookworm or other GI parasites
NSAID use (GI mucosal damage causing silent GI bleeding)
Chronic kidney disease (CKD — reduced erythropoiesis + GI blood loss from uraemia)
Older adults with chronic disease, poor appetite, or GI blood loss
Endurance athletes ('sports anaemia' — increased RBC turnover, foot-strike haemolysis, GI blood loss from exertion)

symptoms.important_note: IDA symptoms are determined by both the degree of anaemia (Hb level) AND the rate of onset. Chronic slow-developing IDA is often remarkably well-tolerated — patients with Hb 7-8 g/dL from slowly progressive IDA may be ambulatory with surprisingly few symptoms as the body has time to compensate (increased cardiac output, rightward shift of oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve via 2,3-DPG increase). Rapidly developing anaemia of equivalent severity causes far more symptoms.

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Weakness (Tiredness)
primary_symptoms.description: The most universal and prominent symptom of IDA — experienced by virtually all patients with significant anaemia. Goes beyond simple tiredness from reduced oxygen delivery — iron deficiency independently impairs mitochondrial energy production (iron is essential for cytochrome enzymes in oxidative phosphorylation) and muscle function (myoglobin reduction). Results in: profound physical exhaustion; reduced exercise tolerance; difficulty performing activities of daily living that were previously effortless; muscle weakness. Characteristically disproportionate to degree of activity — even minimal exertion causes fatigue. Often described as 'bone tiredness' that rest does not fully relieve.
primary_symptoms.onset: Insidious and progressive with chronic IDA
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Fatigue in IDA is both from anaemia (reduced O2 delivery) AND from iron-deficient mitochondrial dysfunction — explains why iron supplementation may not fully resolve fatigue until iron stores are completely replenished (even after Hb normalises)

primary_symptoms.name: Pallor (Paleness)
primary_symptoms.description: Visible pallor from reduced haemoglobin concentration reducing the pink-red colour of blood in superficial vessels. Assessed at: (1) Conjunctivae — pallor of palpebral conjunctiva (lower eyelid lining) is the most reliable clinical sign; (2) Nailbeds — pale pink or white instead of normal pink; (3) Palmar creases — creases normally pink-red; pale or white creases in anaemia; (4) Tongue and oral mucosa — pale; (5) Skin generalised pallor (less reliable — affected by pigmentation). Conjunctival pallor has ~75% sensitivity for Hb <10 g/dL in experienced hands.

primary_symptoms.name: Dyspnoea (Breathlessness) on Exertion
primary_symptoms.description: Exertional breathlessness from reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood — the lungs must increase respiratory rate to compensate for reduced per-breath oxygen delivery. Initially only on strenuous exercise, progressing to normal activities, and in severe anaemia present at rest. Physiologically: reduced blood oxygen content → compensatory tachycardia + increased cardiac output → increased cardiac work + increased ventilation rate.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (on exertion only) to Severe (at rest)

primary_symptoms.name: Palpitations (Awareness of Heartbeat)
primary_symptoms.description: Awareness of the heartbeat — rapid, pounding, or irregular sensations. Results from the compensatory tachycardia and increased cardiac output (high-output state) that the heart develops to maintain tissue oxygen delivery in the face of reduced blood oxygen-carrying capacity. May be continuous at rest in severe anaemia. A haemic systolic flow murmur (grade 1-2/6, heard at the left sternal border) may develop from the turbulent high-output state — disappears with correction of anaemia.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (awareness of heartbeat) to Significant (tachycardia at rest)

primary_symptoms.name: Pica — Craving Non-Food Substances
primary_symptoms.description: Pica is the compulsive consumption of non-nutritive, often inedible substances — a SPECIFIC and PATHOGNOMONIC iron-deficiency symptom (does NOT occur in other anaemias). The most common form in IDA is PAGOPHAGIA — compulsive craving for ice (ice-chewing). Other forms: soil (geophagia — eating clay or soil), laundry starch, chalk, charcoal, hair. Mechanism poorly understood — possible that ice-chewing relieves inflammation in oral mucosa (glossitis); cravings are involuntary and often embarrassing for patients. Pica disappears promptly with iron repletion — its resolution confirms the diagnosis.
primary_symptoms.diagnostic_value: Highly specific for iron deficiency — if present, virtually confirms IDA; disappears with iron treatment

primary_symptoms.name: Koilonychia (Spoon-Shaped Nails)
primary_symptoms.description: A classic iron-specific physical sign — the nail becomes soft and thin, then eventually concave and spoon-shaped (the nail bed scoops upward rather than curving downward normally). In early iron deficiency: nails become brittle, break easily, and have longitudinal ridges. In established IDA: classic spoon shape in which a drop of water placed on the nail does not roll off. Most pronounced in finger nails. Results from iron-deficient nail keratinocyte dysfunction. Koilonychia reverses with iron therapy over several months.
primary_symptoms.diagnostic_specificity: Specific for IDA when present; may also be seen in haemochromatosis (early) and after chemical exposure

secondary_symptoms: Headache — particularly frontal or bitemporal; from cerebral vasodilation compensating for reduced oxygen delivery; more common with acute or severe anaemia
Dizziness and lightheadedness — particularly on standing (orthostatic symptoms from reduced cerebral blood flow); may cause near-syncope or falls in elderly

Poor concentration and cognitive impairment — iron is essential for dopamine D2 receptor function, prefrontal cortex activity, and myelin synthesis; IDA impairs executive function, attention, memory, and learning (very significant in children)

Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) — uncomfortable, irresistible urge to move legs particularly at rest or at night; 25-30% of IDA patients have RLS; iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis in basal ganglia; serum ferritin <50-75 ng/mL is associated with RLS; iron supplementation dramatically improves symptoms
Glossitis — smooth, atrophic, painful tongue; loss of filiform papillae giving a 'beefy red' appearance; burning sensation; iron-specific
Angular stomatitis / Angular cheilitis — painful fissuring and crusting at the corners of the mouth; iron deficiency impairs mucosal epithelial cell turnover
Hair loss and hair thinning — diffuse non-scarring alopecia; iron essential for follicular stem cell function; telogen effluvium (increased hair shedding); responds to iron treatment over 3-6 months
Impaired immune function — iron essential for neutrophil function, T-lymphocyte proliferation, NK cell activity; IDA patients have increased susceptibility to infections

Dysphagia — in severe or longstanding IDA: post-cricoid oesophageal web formation (Plummer-Vinson or Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome — rare but important: associated with postcricoid carcinoma risk; requires endoscopic dilatation and iron treatment)
Cold intolerance — iron deficiency impairs thyroid hormone metabolism and thermoregulation
Irritability and mood changes — particularly in children and adolescents; iron deficiency in the brain affects monoamine neurotransmitter metabolism (serotonin, dopamine)
Reduced appetite in children — creates a vicious cycle of reduced iron intake worsening IDA
Poor wound healing and skin changes — iron required for collagen synthesis; skin may appear dry and brittle
symptoms_specific_to_children: Developmental delay and impaired cognitive development — the most important consequence; iron is critical for myelination, synaptogenesis, and dopaminergic neurodevelopment; early IDA can cause IRREVERSIBLE cognitive deficits even when treated later
Behavioural problems — irritability, reduced attention span, poor performance in school
Reduced physical growth and delayed milestones
Increased susceptibility to infections (recurrent ear infections, respiratory infections)
Breath-holding spells in young children — IDA is a risk factor
Pallor — noted by parents; conjunctival pallor on examination
Pica may manifest as eating soil, paint, paper, or other non-food items

plummer_vinson_syndrome.description: A triad of: (1) Dysphagia (from post-cricoid oesophageal web); (2) Iron deficiency anaemia; (3) Atrophic glossitis. Predominantly in middle-aged women. Associated with increased risk of postcricoid squamous cell carcinoma. Treat with iron + endoscopic web dilatation + regular endoscopic surveillance.

diagnostic_approach.overview: IDA diagnosis requires two steps: (1) Confirm anaemia and iron deficiency (blood tests — FBC, iron studies, ferritin); (2) Identify the underlying cause (history, examination, and directed investigations). Never stop at confirming IDA without investigating the underlying cause — in adults (especially men and postmenopausal women), IDA may be the presenting sign of an occult malignancy.

medical_history: Dietary history: meat, fish, poultry consumption; vegetarian/vegan diet; milk intake in children; fortified food consumption; Vitamin C intake (enhancer); tea/coffee with meals (inhibitors)
Menstrual history: cycle regularity; duration; passage of clots; number of pads/tampons per day; impact on daily activities (menorrhagia assessment — pictorial blood assessment chart)
Gastrointestinal symptoms: rectal bleeding; blood in stool (bright red or melaena); change in bowel habit; abdominal pain; dysphagia; heartburn; weight loss (malignancy); diarrhoea (coeliac, IBD)
Haematological history: family history of anaemia or haemoglobinopathy; history of similar anaemia in past; response to iron supplements before
Medication history: NSAIDs (GI bleeding); aspirin; anticoagulants; PPIs (reduce iron absorption); methotrexate; iron supplements (current and compliance)
Obstetric history: number of pregnancies and deliveries; postpartum haemorrhage; breastfeeding
Surgical history: gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, bowel resection, colectomy
Symptoms of iron deficiency: pica (ice craving, clay eating); restless legs; hair loss; glossitis; dysphagia; nail changes (koilonychia)
Symptoms of underlying cause: weight loss; night sweats; altered bowel habit; rectal bleeding; post-menopausal bleeding; haematuria
Social history: geographic exposure (hookworm endemic areas — India); vegetarianism; food insecurity; alcohol (GI bleeding, nutritional impact)
Family history: coeliac disease; GI malignancy; hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
physical_examination: Vital signs: HR (tachycardia in moderate-severe anaemia); blood pressure; respiratory rate; oxygen saturation
General appearance: pallor (generalised); fatigue appearance; body habitus (weight loss suggests malignancy or malabsorption)
Eyes: conjunctival pallor — lower lid pulled down; normal pale pink vs pallor; jaundice sclera (haemolytic anaemia differential)
Nails and hands: koilonychia (spoon nails); pallor of nail beds; brittle nails; longitudinal ridging; palmar crease pallor (palmar creases pallor in severe anaemia)
Mouth and tongue: angular stomatitis (cheilitis); glossitis (smooth red tongue — loss of papillae); oral candidiasis (from immune impairment)
Abdominal examination: splenomegaly (mild in haemolytic anaemia — not IDA; but suggests differential); hepatomegaly; rectal examination (haemorrhoids; melaena on glove — GI blood loss)

Cardiovascular: heart rate and rhythm; haemic systolic flow murmur (grade 1-2/6 at left sternal border; soft, ejection; disappears with Hb correction); signs of heart failure (very severe anaemia: raised JVP, oedema, bibasal crackles — high-output failure)
Neurological: cognitive assessment in children (developmental milestones); signs of peripheral neuropathy (B12 deficiency differential)
Skin: koilonychia; hair thinning or hair loss (alopecia); skin pallor; dry and brittle skin
Lymph nodes: lymphadenopathy (malignancy differential in unexplained anaemia)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) with Red Cell Indices
diagnostic_tests.description: The cornerstone initial investigation. In IDA: Haemoglobin (Hb) low; Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) low (<80 fL — microcytosis); Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin (MCH) low (<27 pg — hypochromia); Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC) low (<320 g/L); Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW) high (>14.5% — anisocytosis, reflecting mixed population of normal and microcytic cells); Platelet count often elevated (reactive thrombocytosis) in IDA from ongoing blood loss.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm anaemia; characterise as microcytic hypochromic (IDA morphology); assess severity (Hb level); calculate red cell indices; detect reactive thrombocytosis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hb <12 g/dL (women) or <13 g/dL (men) + MCV <80 fL + MCH <27 pg = microcytic hypochromic anaemia (IDA morphology). RDW elevated in IDA (anisocytosis). Platelets often elevated in bleeding-related IDA.
diagnostic_tests.differential_MCV: Low MCV (microcytic): IDA; Thalassaemia; Anaemia of chronic disease (usually normocytic but can be mildly microcytic); Lead poisoning; Sideroblastic anaemia. Normal MCV (normocytic): ACD; mixed IDA + B12/folate deficiency; renal anaemia; acute blood loss. High MCV (macrocytic): B12 or folate deficiency; liver disease; hypothyroidism

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Peripheral Blood Film (PBF) Examination
diagnostic_tests.description: Manual examination of blood smear under microscope — provides qualitative assessment of red cell morphology. In IDA: (1) Microcytes (small red cells); (2) Hypochromia (cells appear pale/ghost-like with enlarged central pallor >1/3 cell diameter); (3) Pencil cells (elliptocytes/cigar cells — elongated red cells specific to IDA); (4) Target cells (central dense area with pallor halo); (5) Anisocytosis (variable size — high RDW); (6) Poikilocytosis (variable shape). Pencil cells (pencil poikilocytes) are a classic and specific IDA finding.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm hypochromic microcytic morphology; identify specific IDA morphological features (pencil cells); exclude other haematological diagnoses (haemolysis, dysplasia)
diagnostic_tests.key_findings: Pencil cells/poikilocytes: highly characteristic of IDA; Hypochromia + microcytes: confirms morphology; absence of these suggests thalassaemia or ACD

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Ferritin
diagnostic_tests.type: Blood — Most Sensitive and Specific Test for Iron Stores
diagnostic_tests.description: The single most important test for diagnosing iron deficiency. Ferritin is the iron storage protein — serum ferritin reflects body iron stores. A LOW serum ferritin is the MOST SPECIFIC indicator of iron deficiency. CAVEAT: ferritin is an acute phase reactant — it is FALSELY ELEVATED in inflammation, infection, liver disease, malignancy, and chronic disease — meaning iron deficiency may coexist with a 'normal' or even elevated ferritin in these conditions. When ferritin is in the 30-100 ng/mL range with inflammation, use other markers (sTfR, sTfR/log ferritin ratio, zinc protoporphyrin) to assess iron deficiency.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Gold standard for iron store assessment; first-line test for IDA diagnosis; monitor treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ferritin <12 ng/mL: CONFIRMED iron deficiency (specific); <30 ng/mL: iron deficiency (sensitive); 30-100 ng/mL with inflammation: possible iron deficiency (use sTfR to confirm); Normal: 12-150 ng/mL women; 12-300 ng/mL men
diagnostic_tests.treatment_target: Replenish stores to ferritin >50-100 ng/mL (not just normalising Hb) to ensure complete symptom resolution including fatigue and restless legs

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Iron, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC), and Transferrin Saturation
diagnostic_tests.description: A panel of tests reflecting plasma iron transport. In IDA: Serum iron LOW (<60 µg/dL); TIBC HIGH (>400 µg/dL — liver produces more transferrin to maximise iron capture); Transferrin saturation LOW (<16%). In Anaemia of Chronic Disease (ACD): Serum iron LOW; TIBC NORMAL or LOW; Transferrin saturation LOW — distinguishes from IDA where TIBC is characteristically HIGH.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm iron deficiency pattern; distinguish IDA from ACD; assess iron transport
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: IDA pattern: Serum iron <60 µg/dL + TIBC >400 µg/dL + Transferrin saturation <16%; ACD pattern: Low iron + LOW/normal TIBC + low transferrin saturation
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Serum iron highly variable — diurnal variation (highest morning); affected by recent oral iron intake; meals; inflammation — less reliable than ferritin as sole test

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Reticulocyte Count and Reticulocyte Haemoglobin Content (CHr / RetHe)
diagnostic_tests.description: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells released from bone marrow — normally 0.5-2% of RBCs. In IDA: reticulocyte count LOW or NORMAL (iron-restricted erythropoiesis reduces new RBC production). After iron treatment is started: reticulocyte count RISES sharply (reticulocytosis peak at 7-10 days) — this reticulocyte response confirms the diagnosis of IDA and confirms response to iron therapy. Reticulocyte Haemoglobin Content (CHr/RetHe): the haemoglobin content of individual reticulocytes — low CHr (<28 pg) is an early and sensitive marker of iron-deficient erythropoiesis — identifies functional iron deficiency before anaemia develops.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess erythropoiesis; monitor iron treatment response (reticulocytosis by day 7-10); detect functional iron deficiency early (CHr)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Reticulocyte count: low/normal in IDA; peak reticulocytosis (3-5% or higher) at day 7-10 after iron treatment = confirms IDA diagnosis and treatment response; CHr <28 pg = iron-deficient erythropoiesis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Soluble Transferrin Receptor (sTfR) and sTfR/Log Ferritin Ratio
diagnostic_tests.description: Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) is expressed on erythroid precursor cells and internalises transferrin-iron complexes for Hb synthesis. When iron supply is inadequate, cells upregulate TfR1 expression — a soluble form (sTfR) is shed into serum. sTfR rises in iron deficiency (iron-starved erythroid cells increase TfR1). UNIQUE ADVANTAGE: sTfR is NOT an acute phase reactant — it is RELIABLE even in the presence of inflammation, making it the test of choice to diagnose iron deficiency in patients with inflammatory conditions where ferritin is falsely elevated.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose iron deficiency in presence of inflammation/chronic disease (ACD vs IDA distinction); sTfR/log ferritin ratio (Thomas Plot) provides accurate assessment of iron stores even in inflammatory states
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: sTfR elevated in IDA (>1.8-2.2 mg/L depending on assay); normal in ACD; sTfR/log ferritin >2.0 suggests absolute iron deficiency even with normal/elevated ferritin

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Coeliac Disease Serology (Anti-TTG IgA + Total IgA)
diagnostic_tests.description: NICE guidelines (UK) and ACG recommend coeliac serology in ALL patients with IDA — coeliac disease is present in up to 5% of IDA patients and the IDA may be the only presenting feature. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (Anti-TTG IgA) is the first-line test. Total IgA must also be checked to exclude IgA deficiency (which gives a false negative TTG IgA).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude coeliac disease as cause of malabsorption IDA; mandatory screen in all IDA patients
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive TTG IgA (>10 U/mL or >3x ULN): investigate with upper GI endoscopy + duodenal biopsies; if IgA deficient: use TTG IgG or deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies (DGP IgG)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: H. pylori Testing (Urea Breath Test / Stool Antigen / Serology)
diagnostic_tests.description: H. pylori should be tested and treated in patients with IDA, particularly: unexplained IDA; IDA resistant to oral iron therapy; IDA in the absence of another identified cause. H. pylori eradication has been shown to improve IDA independent of GI blood loss from ulcers — through improved iron absorption and reduced competition for iron.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify H. pylori as cause of IDA (treatment and eradication improves IDA); investigate as part of GI cause investigation
diagnostic_tests.tests: Urea breath test (most accurate non-invasive — must stop PPIs 2 weeks before); Stool antigen test; Endoscopic biopsy with rapid urease test (CLO test) if upper GI endoscopy performed

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Upper GI Endoscopy (Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy — OGD)
diagnostic_tests.type: Endoscopic — MANDATORY in Men and Postmenopausal Women
diagnostic_tests.description: Upper GI endoscopy is MANDATORY in ALL men and ALL postmenopausal women with IDA to exclude upper GI malignancy (gastric cancer, oesophageal cancer), peptic ulcer disease (H. pylori/NSAID-related), gastric or duodenal erosions, angiodysplasia, oesophageal varices, and Barrett's oesophagus. During OGD: duodenal biopsies taken to screen for coeliac disease (important cause of malabsorption IDA).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude upper GI malignancy; diagnose peptic ulcer disease; take duodenal biopsies for coeliac disease; identify angiodysplasia
diagnostic_tests.mandatory_in: All men with IDA; all postmenopausal women with IDA; premenopausal women with IDA and GI symptoms or inadequate response to iron

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Colonoscopy (Lower GI Endoscopy)
diagnostic_tests.type: Endoscopic — MANDATORY in Men and Postmenopausal Women
diagnostic_tests.description: Colonoscopy is MANDATORY in ALL men and postmenopausal women with IDA — colorectal cancer can cause occult GI blood loss presenting ONLY as IDA with no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no abdominal pain. Colonoscopy allows direct visualisation of the entire colon, detection of polyps, tumours, and angiodysplasia. A 'two-week wait' urgent referral for suspected colorectal cancer should be made when IDA is found in a man or postmenopausal woman.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude colorectal cancer (urgent — IDA is a presentation of colorectal cancer); diagnose IBD, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, polyps
diagnostic_tests.mandatory_in: All men with IDA; all postmenopausal women with IDA — NICE guidelines (UK 2021)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Faecal Occult Blood Test (FOBT) / Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT)
diagnostic_tests.description: Detects hidden (occult) blood in stool — useful when colonoscopy not yet available or to triage urgency. FIT (immunochemical — detects human haemoglobin specifically) is superior to guaiac FOBT (detects haem from any source including dietary meat). Positive FIT in IDA further supports GI blood loss.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for GI blood loss; triage urgency of colonoscopy; colorectal cancer screening adjunct
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Does NOT exclude colorectal cancer if negative — colonoscopy is required regardless in high-risk patients

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Thyroid Function Tests (TSH)
diagnostic_tests.description: Hypothyroidism can cause anaemia (macrocytic — from B12 deficiency) AND worsen iron utilisation. Also relevant when fatigue is disproportionate to anaemia severity. Screen in patients with IDA + unexplained fatigue + other hypothyroid features.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude hypothyroidism as contributing cause of anaemia or disproportionate fatigue

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Haemoglobin Electrophoresis / HPLC (High-Performance Liquid Chromatography)
diagnostic_tests.description: Distinguishes IDA from thalassaemia (both cause microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low MCV) and haemoglobinopathies. Thalassaemia trait is very common in India and South Asia — may coexist with IDA or be misdiagnosed as IDA. Thalassaemia has: very low MCV with relatively normal Hb; elevated HbA2 (beta-thalassaemia trait — HbA2 >3.5%); normal or elevated ferritin; RDW normal (vs elevated in IDA). HPLC is the gold standard for haemoglobin variant identification.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Differentiate IDA from thalassaemia trait/disease (critical before IV iron or blood transfusion); identify haemoglobin variants (HbS, HbE, HbC)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Beta-thalassaemia trait: HbA2 >3.5%; HbF variable; normal or elevated ferritin; Alpha-thalassaemia trait: normal HPLC (diagnosis by molecular testing)
diagnostic_tests.india_context: Thalassaemia is highly prevalent in India — always exclude before treating IDA aggressively

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Pelvic Ultrasound and Gynaecological Assessment
diagnostic_tests.description: In premenopausal women with IDA from suspected menorrhagia — transvaginal or transabdominal pelvic ultrasound identifies: uterine fibroids, adenomyosis, endometrial thickening, ovarian pathology. Essential before treating menorrhagia medically or surgically.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify structural cause of menorrhagia (fibroids, adenomyosis) causing IDA in women

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Bone Marrow Aspiration and Trephine Biopsy (Rare — Gold Standard)
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard for iron deficiency diagnosis (absence of stainable iron on Prussian blue stain = iron deficiency) but rarely needed clinically — reserved for complex cases where diagnosis is uncertain after all non-invasive investigations. Also indicated when IDA fails to respond to treatment and cause remains obscure, or when bone marrow disorder (myelodysplastic syndrome, aplastic anaemia) is suspected as a concomitant diagnosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Gold standard diagnosis when other tests inconclusive; exclude marrow failure; distinguish IDA from ACD definitively
diagnostic_tests.prussian_blue_stain: Absence of haemosiderin/ferritin granules in macrophages = absolute iron deficiency; confirms IDA

treatment_principles: 1. Always investigate and treat the UNDERLYING CAUSE — iron supplementation alone is insufficient if ongoing blood loss continues
2. Oral iron is first-line for most patients — ferrous salts (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate) are best absorbed

3. IV iron when: oral not tolerated; malabsorption (coeliac, bariatric surgery); ongoing blood loss faster than oral can replace; pregnancy (2nd/3rd trimester when rapid correction needed); inflammatory conditions with impaired oral absorption
4. Blood transfusion reserved for: Hb <7 g/dL with symptoms; pre-operative haemodynamic instability; severe cardiac compromise — NOT for uncomplicated mild-moderate IDA
5. Target ferritin >50-100 ng/mL (not just Hb normalisation) — full store repletion required to resolve all symptoms especially fatigue and restless legs
6. Continue oral iron for 3-6 months AFTER Hb normalises to replenish iron stores

medications.note: Iron repletion is the definitive treatment for IDA. The choice between oral and IV iron depends on: severity, tolerance, cause (malabsorption), urgency, and patient preference. The underlying CAUSE must be treated simultaneously — iron supplementation alone is palliative if the cause continues. All iron supplements should be prescribed by a licensed physician. Children's doses are weight-based — never guess doses for children.
